reader_summary.headline: Jeff Totten shares lessons from Home Depot and his own acquisition strategy.
reader_summary.overview: Jeff Totten discusses building a long-term holding company similar to Berkshire Hathaway. He learned from the Home Depot founders to focus on one industry, trust local leaders, and make hard foundational investments. His team prioritizes recurring revenue and customer trust over quick profits.

key_points.text: Jeff started by selling digital photos and learned that buying companies is a powerful way to build a business.
key_points.evidence_quote: I came across Warren Buffett and in the books snowball about Buffett. And that's when it really clicked for me this idea of building companies through acquisitions.

key_points.text: The company built expertise in IT services and ERP software, using knowledge from one area to improve the others.
key_points.evidence_quote: So really the way we built the business over time is we've established three verticals. MSPs are the big vertical that we started with and a fully outsourced IT for all businesses.

key_points.text: A major early mistake was trying to fully integrate a bought company instead of keeping its own brand and CEO.
key_points.evidence_quote: We bought a company that had an existing M&A strategy that was quite a bit different from how we were doing acquisitions. We were doing acquisitions on a decentralized basis.

key_points.text: Leaders measure success by recurring revenue growth, profit margins, and keeping customers happy over many years rather than just quick sales.
key_points.evidence_quote: We focus both on top line growth. Are we seeing particularly recurring revenue growth in our businesses? We focus on margins and is that top line growth dropping to the bottom line?

key_points.text: The company believes it is foolish to make short-term money if it hurts the long-term trust and relationship with a customer.
key_points.evidence_quote: It is economically foolish to do something in the short term that might make you an extra dollar that in any way, you know, threatens the trust that that customer has with our business.

transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
I'm your host Edipalmian and today we're delighted to have Jeff Totten on the show.
Jeff is the founder and CEO of Evergreen Services Group,
a holding company for technology services businesses.
The firm is based in San Francisco and has done over 160 acquisitions in its first nine years,
currently generating about $1.5 billion in revenue.
For this episode, Jeff has selected the book Build From Scratch,
how a couple of regular guys grew the home depot from nothing to $30 billion.
I really like this book, which is written by the founders of Home Depot
and I think it proves how far common sense can take you,
but also the many challenges along the way to success.
Build From Scratch was published in 1999 and we're thrilled to discuss it on the show today.
Here comes our conversation with Jeff Totten.
Hi Jeff and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast.
How are you? Good to see you.
It's great to have you on.
We recently met in Stockholm at Red Eye Serial Aquarius Conference,
where are we reaching you today?
I'm in Minnesota, so all the colder than home base, which is San Francisco.
Very good and to begin, I'm curious about your upbringing
and how this has shaped you as a person.
Yeah, so I grew up in the Bay Area and you're close by where the company is based today in San Francisco.
And my dad was an entrepreneur.
He had a construction company and I always looked up to him.
He was kind of my role model growing up and I wanted to be a business leader and entrepreneur like he was.
And so in high school, I started a photography company.
I was interested in photography and decided to turn that into a business.
I would go and take pictures at, you know, high school events could be a sporting event or Eagle Scout event.
And I would sell digital downloads to the parents, which is a very easy audience to sell sell to.
I'd sell, you know, mostly to my friends parents.
But that's how I got into business.
And from there, you know, I get interested in, hey, how do you build a business app?
And so I went to the bookstore and grabbed every book off the shelf that you talked about business.
And there happened to be some books on investing that were right next to the books on on running a business.
And so that's when I came across Warren Buffett and in the books snowball about Buffett.
And that's when it really clicked for me this idea of building companies through acquisitions.
And so it really been interested in it since I would say high school when I first discovered a fit in the power of acquiring companies and operating companies and being an entrepreneur.
And how much investing have you done like on the private side and investing in in public companies for your own sake since since those days.
I've been investing since I was in high school and it was a fascinating time.
You know, this was during the great financial crisis. So it was a fascinating time to start investing.
Obviously it's a good time to start investing when stocks are pretty low.
You can you can feel pretty good about how you're doing when it's stocks are at a low during my lifetime.
Through that, it was also an interesting time to read about, you know, what makes businesses durable and able to survive recession.
But also, you know, some of the things that people get wrong running businesses, it can cause them to go out of business.
So I've been investing in public companies since, since high school and then on the private side, I got into private equity directly out of undergrad and invested both through the private equity firm.
And then I also personally invested in several search funds during that period of time.
So I got exposure both personally and professionally to private investments directly out of undergrad.
And nine years ago in 2017, you found that Evergreen Services Group, where you're still the CEO, can you tell a bit about,
we'll get into the business and how this has formed. But can you say a bit more about how this came about?
And my co founder Ramsey and myself, we were both working at a private equity firm called Alpine investors and really a pretty innovative private equity firm and one that's had a lot of success with buy and builds and with backing early talent into companies.
And we loved the whole model of acquiring middle market businesses and helping them grow.
So we enjoyed that part of the work within private equity.
But we also really admired Berkshire Hathaway and we went to the meeting in 2017, just saw what Berkshire built over 50 plus years and we're really impressed by that.
And one of the things that stood out is just the power of the holding company structure, the idea that the company doesn't have a lifetime, similar to how a private equity fund has a lifetime to it.
And we thought, hey, that's the right structure to build in for us, like we wanted to do something over many decades, we wanted our work to be cumulative, not a project based.
And so we proposed the idea to Alpine going back from the Berkshire annual meeting, what if we built something similar to Berkshire backed by Alpine.
And that was our big audacious idea. And Alpine supported us, they backed early talent and they supported us and getting this off the ground with their backing.
It took a few weeks after we got back from the meeting to have the initial commitment from Alpine and the one piece of advice they gave us is, you know, we know you want to build Berkshire Hathaway long term but start by focusing on a single industry.
And so we decided to focus it on the managed IT industry to start and that's our foundation as a company.
Amazing. And how old are you now and what stage of life do you feel like you're in and how is that for you now?
I'm mid 30s, my wife and I are starting our family, I'll actually all the partners evergreen or every since recently started their families.
And I find it to be a very fun point to be building and to be a leader in a company we've been doing it for eight, nine years.
So I think we've made some mistakes and learn from those mistakes, we've got some experience.
But at the same time, you know, we're very early in our in what we're building like we feel like this is just getting started.
And so we feel like we can look build upon upon that over the next, you know, several decades as a company.
So in some ways it feels like, you know, we're evergreen we've scaled to a billion and a half dollars of revenue.
It feels like it could be a mature company.
A lot of ways it feels like we're just really at the beginning of building the business right now.
And today we'll speak about the book that is also starting something from the beginning.
It's called Build From Scratch.
Can you briefly tell us what is this book about?
Yeah, it's about the founding of Home Depot and really the first 20 years of the business being built.
And it's written by the founders.
So that's one of my favorite parts about the book is that it's a first hand story.
You know, Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank telling the story of building the business truly from scratch.
And it's it's a more entrepreneurial story than you would expect.
Home Depot today is a big business.
But really they started by trying to raise a few million dollars and built the business from the ground up.
And it ended up being a very entrepreneurial business is the way that they built.
I think that really comes through in the book as you read through some of the stories in the book.
And I think what's surprising about it, people think about Home Depot, they think of a national brand.
I think more consistency across all the stores, but it's actually a highly decentralized business,
at least in how is built by the founders, which is comparable to how we're building evergreen.
So I found it to be a very enjoyable book, a very impressive entrepreneurial story.
When did you first come across the book and why did you select it for this episode?
Yeah, well, you made it kind of hard to select a good book because you've you've profiled so many good books that I love.
You know, my favorite book is The Outsiders by Old Thorn Dyke, but you got you had will on for that.
So I had to go deeper down the list, but this is one of my favorite books actually.
It's barely recently actually after my son was born.
I remember reading it while he was napping in our nursery.
So it was an interesting time to be reading it because every was established at that point.
And a new business in its formative years.
I think I was thinking a lot about how to scale our learnings in the business scale or culture in that period of time.
And so it came at a good time from that standpoint that they get about.
How do we kind of take the culture that's working for us at Evergreen and really scaled up and how do I need to evolve as a leader.
And I think the fact that it's 20 years into the journey is when the book was written.
It's really relevant because I was in your six, seven when I read it.
And in build to scratch, we learned that one of the role models for Home Depot was Walmart.
So in your way of building Evergreen, which companies do you look up to for inspiration?
Well, the superodacious one is Berkshire Hathaway and naturally, and that was inspiration.
But a little closer.
Where we are, but still far ahead of us are.
You know, on the acquisitions that we look a lot at, you know, Constellation software.
We look at the great Swedish serial acquires that we are profiled at the red eye.
Our friends, those like businesses that inspires from a capital discipline standpoint from an acquisition strategy standpoint.
And then on the, on more of the how to create value in our commission.
Part of our strategies, how do we acquire businesses, hold them forever be a great home for them.
Another part of our strategies, and we create as much value as possible in the businesses that we own.
And there we really look at look at the trans dime as an example company that's through the three P's playbook of value creation.
So that's another role model that we have in a company that we pay close attention to.
And if you look at Berkshire, they can basically invest in anything.
And you mentioned you have focused to begin with at least in one sector or area.
Why was that and can you speak a bit more about the type of companies that you want to own?
I think when you think about where we play in the market, we play far down market.
And so if we had to get up to speed every time we bought a company, it'd be very hard to operate at the pace that we operate.
We acquired over 160 businesses over the past eight to nine years.
And I think it would just create too much risk for us as a company to begin up to speed on a new business every time.
And after we acquire the businesses, we're trying to create value in those businesses.
So this value to kind of in cumulative learnings from each acquisition should make us better at acquiring businesses in our space.
She also make us better operating businesses in our space.
And so that was a core principle from the GICGO and really important and valuable advice that Alpine gave us to focus.
So really the way we built the business over time is we've established three verticals.
MSPs are the big vertical that we started with and a fully outsourced IT for all businesses.
Then we got into implementing ERP software, which is basically accounting software for middle market companies.
And then the last industry is government IT services.
So on, they're all under this broader kind of technology services umbrella.
And there's, you know, there's knowledge we have from MSPs that made us better at buying ERP partners.
This knowledge from ERP partners that made us better at buying government IT.
And we will expand our mandate over time.
I don't ever see us buying kind of a hodgepodge of businesses when we go into a vertical.
We want to make multiple acquisitions and we want to become experts in that vertical.
And if we go into lessons from the book, the founders before starting Home Depot,
they got fired from their previous jobs.
And that's quite early in the book.
That was of course very tough for them but turned out eventually to be a blessing considering what they built.
I'm wondering if there have been any such pivotal moments for you during the journey with Abergrin?
Well, the founding was pivotal was pivotal.
I'm not that because we got fired.
I mean, Alpine backed us and supported our vision from the get go.
But that leap of faith that Alpine took on us was a big deal.
And it put us into business when we were in our mid 20s at the time.
So that that was a really pivotal moment.
We're from an adversity standpoint.
I'd say a pivotal moment was in our first year.
We bought a company that had an existing M&A strategy that was quite a bit different from how we were doing acquisitions.
We were doing acquisitions on a decentralized basis.
So each business we acquired kept its own brand, its own CEO.
And this business had a successful track record of buying businesses and fully integrating them into their platform.
And so our thought was, hey, let's keep that going.
In fact, with our scale, why don't we accelerate how much M&A that they're doing.
And that turned out to be a bad strategy for us.
It turns out when you're doing that level of integration and you're changing up the management team.
You can't move as fast as we were trying to move.
And there was some cracks in the foundation of what we're what we acquired, particularly when you put that much stress that many acquisitions on top of it.
And that was our first year of starting the company.
And so it was, you know, a pretty risky moment for the business.
We paused acquisitions at that company, you know, we got, you know, we got that business to a stable point and we pressed ahead and building the business.
And it was, you know, what we had to look at is we're trying to build this business over multiple decades.
We had a very big vision for the company.
And we, Ramsey, my view is there's only way that we could move forward was aiming towards that vision, continuing to buy quality businesses outside of this company in the performance stabilized and really driving organic growth at our other companies.
And it was kind of a critical moment where we just had to lock in in that first year.
And so we have an unusual story in that we did more M&A in that first year than we did in the second year, as you tried to get things back on track.
And then from there, it's been a really fast growth experience.
But we, you know, it was a tough moment for us to make it, you know, very early on where we weren't sure how that was going to turn out for the business.
It was really clear from the book that when you're young, you're very vulnerable.
And you mentioned the funding and being backed by Alpan was really important for you.
And in the book, they had a lot of struggles with that as well, how to find capital.
Can you share some stories from the book how they did actually raise capital to fund the business in the early days of Home Depot?
It was a long time ago, but it was, it was a pretty small, even I think by the time standards, it was not a very big capital is like a couple of a few million dollars or trying to raise.
And they had a, there's a very important person who wrote a server book, Kendlyn Goan, who's their investment banker, really almost served as a third founder of the business alongside them.
And he helped arrange financing for them. And in multiple times, they got pretty far along with investors and, you know, the founders, Bernie and Arthur decided to pull out because there wasn't value alignment.
In one case, it was Ross Perot and they, he said, my people don't drive Cadillacs and they happen to have like a use, the founders of Home Depot happen to have a use Cadillac that they drove for work.
And that was a signal that after the investment was going to happen, he was going to have more, that investors, you have more say over how they run the business and they wanted a partner that trusted them.
So they worked through multiple iterations to that until they finally found an investor base that it was more aligned with what they were trying to build. And I think it was going out to much smaller investors, a more diversified group of investors to back them.
I think I think the big learning from that, that moment for Home Depot was really making sure everyone you partner with, you know, from a financing standpoint, investor standpoint.
And keep people in the business has to be values lines and has to believe in you and there has to be trust out of across the board.
I thought it was actually quite impressive, you know, at moments where they seem like they were on the brink of, you know, be able to raise fundraiser, raise the capital that they needed, they pulled out because they saw some little sign that they weren't values align with their investors.
And I think that's hard to do when you're starting a brand new company and you're very close to the finish line.
So I think incredible to them and in our business, it's something we really focus on. Are we aligned with people that were partnered with the business leaders of the companies, our financing partners, our investors, the business owners that we acquire companies from.
You just need to have that alignment across the board because life's too short to build people that aren't aligned with you.
And speaking about that alignment, it's as you say, it's not only about funding, it's about many other things as well.
And in the book, we read that the founders of people really say, like, culture, you can't just delegate culture.
It's something that they must personally carry and transmit. And this has to be on from the get go.
So how do you think about culture and philosophy at every green and aligning that with everyone?
We're definitely structured a lot differently than Home Depot. We're not a single national brand, right?
So we do one of our core values that evergreen is empowerment.
And therefore we let our companies have their own cultures. Now those cultures generally only work if there's, you know, some sort of alignment with evergreen's values that they were not going to buy businesses from.
We don't have a high level alignment with evergreen from a cultural values standpoint.
We don't, we buy the company, we don't change the values, we let the team locally set their own values.
And so we're a little bit different how we're structured from that regard.
But I think what the evergreen culture, it's about, you know, we're decentralized.
And so we're very focused on empowering our leaders to run their businesses as if they're running an independent venture that they started.
And that's really important. We think that's how you get outsized results in these small businesses.
Next we, we are very focused on persistence and that that really started with Ramsey me starting the business and going out and finding our first acquisition opportunities.
We found that the only way to be successful when we were in our mid 20s and trying to build the business was to just keep after it when whenever business owners rejected us or deal didn't work out the way I wanted to or that early challenged acquisition that we had.
We just had to keep going and keep pressing ahead until we got the results that we're looking for and mentality kind of is pervasive across our group of companies, whether you're a CEO, running an operating company, whether you're on our mna team, trying to make an acquisition or whether you're a frontline technician serving the customer.
We keep going until we get the results that we're looking for.
And the last part of our culture, which is probably a bit more unique is just our long term orientation and our core value associated with that we call it rolling snowballs.
And what we mean by that and snowballs a book that I really love about Warren buffet, but that we mean by rolling snowballs is you have to do some hard work to roll snowball off of a steep hill.
First you have to climb to the top of the hill and you have to compact a snowball to make sure you got a good foundation and then you roll that snowball down the hill and you got to let it go all the way to the bottom.
It gets bigger and bigger as it goes down to the bottom of the hill is it picks up more and more snow.
And that's really what we try and do in our business we're trying to make that's our business we make investments that require a lot of work from a foundational standpoint to get up and running.
We might not be the type of investments you would make if you were a traditional private equity company with a five year old period.
For us we're willing to make these upfront investments, you know, compact the snowball and roll it on the very long hill.
And the other thing is to not interrupt compounding you don't want to stop the snowball halfway down the hill when it's not nearly the full size that you get to make that one more tangible.
Well, you know, an example we announced actually as we're recording this today that we're launching a brand new company to be an AI native business that will be within our pine service group company, which is our ERP business.
And that world there's a lot of people coming that are thinking about how do I have a AI native ERP solution and they're going to think through which partner they want to choose to implement that ERP solution.
Instead of just trying to slightly modify one of our existing businesses, we launched an entirely new company, provide that service.
And that might that investment might not end out over a traditional private equity hold period.
I think over the next 10, 15, 20 years we'll build something really special that business.
And that's a that's a small example of kind of in our culture how we roll snowballs, you know, ideally every quarter.
And when it comes to decentralization, this is of course a key word for many of the Swedish Sea of Aquarius and many others.
In Home Depot, as you mentioned, they were having this system in the business quite naturally.
They wanted the autonomy from for the store managers to take the best decisions.
But I found it funny that they didn't the door to the headquarters of Home Depot.
They didn't say headquarters. They said store support centers were really just wanted to be there for for the stores.
And they spent so much time at the founders, they spent so much time in the stores.
I think it was 60% of the time or something that mentioned.
But of course they have to delegate some things.
But is there something in evergreen that you could never delegate to someone?
Well, first off, the store support center was one of my favorite parts of the book.
The fact that they named their corporate headquarters, the store support, I sent that around to the company after I read the book because I just I love that.
It truly made the store top of the hierarchy as opposed to making corporate the top of the hierarchy and so many companies corporate at the top of the hierarchy for all the wrong reasons.
I love that aspect of the book and also in reading this book, I didn't realize when I picked it up reading about Home Depot with a national brand.
It would be such a decentralized company.
I've been a fan of decentralization for a long time.
I was surprised to learn about decentralization and a book about a national brand company like Home Depot.
So it's pretty pretty unique.
So do your question in terms of what we won't delegate the holding company level.
We do centralized capital allocation and that it's less about not trusting you are operating companies or the verticals to allocate capital.
It's more about just focus that we really want our operating companies and our verticals to be very focused on organic growth.
And we think that oftentimes if you delegate M&A out too far into the organization, M&A is exciting and it tends to be where people want to spend their time.
Often people take their eye off the ball on the really important work of serving the customer of driving organic growth.
And so we've centralized M&A in part because we want to have a strong competency on a central basis.
Part because Ramsey and I just personally love doing M&A and we want we want to drive that kind of work.
One of the things we forgot after we launched the company was the power of keeping all of the operating companies and verticals highly focused on organic growth.
And so we hold that very dear.
We share most other responsibilities or fully delegate other responsibilities to operating companies.
Data operations, the majority of God data strategy all lives at the operating companies.
Any shared functions like finance and accounting or talent acquisition for the CEOs, you have some resources at the holding company to help out with that.
But still most of it happens that the verticals are at the operating companies.
So really, you know, I think by the best way to explain it is, you know, we have over 6000 employees at the operating companies.
We only have 50 at the holding company.
And those 50 are pretty focused on M&A and a few kind of reporting in key talent roles.
But it's it's a pretty limited that we really try to limit the subset of things we focus on it at the holding company and make sure we're very good at those things.
And then we delegate the rest to the operating companies.
And you mentioned that organic growth is important for you.
What are the type of metrics to have or how do you evaluate whether an operator in your in your group is performing as you wanted to.
Yeah, that will get organic growth is central.
And we focus both on top line growth. Are we seeing particularly recurring revenue growth in our businesses?
We focus on margins and is that top line growth dropping to the bottom line? Those are very important.
And then we also focus on this just underlying health of the business. So retention is a very critical metric there net revenue retention customer attention.
Gross revenue retention of things that we focus on.
I think that's an area where a lot of private equity back businesses in our space have struggled because they have centralized a lot of functions gotten further removed from the customer.
And we hold those metrics very dear and we believe that decentralization supports those metrics.
We also pay close attention to employee MPS and customer MPS and again, these are metrics that maybe they don't move the needle on bottom line growth this year.
When you're trying to build a multi decade hopefully a multi century company.
You have to make sure that employees are happy and the thing with the Home Depot story that employees being happy with central delivering a great service over the long haul.
We pay a lot of attention there. And right now, you know, a lot of our putting a lot of focus on innovation and AI is transformative to our business and we're thinking about.
Are we being bold enough in terms of making bets within our companies that will transform the model in terms of our value proposition, our level of efficiency in our companies and also the revenue that we're generating from AI in our businesses.
And customer MPS is one of the metrics there and in the chapter about customers in the book.
It's very clear that Home Depot, they will do whatever it takes to please their customers.
They, one example was that they even gave money back for tires that someone bought and came back with to a store.
And they are not selling tires and they never had so they never sold tires, but they just wanted to make this customer happy and come back.
What do you think about this? Should you really serve every customer everything they want?
Such a great story. One of like one of a few in there where they really, they took on short term expenses or, you know, they let revenue surpass that they could have captured if they're solely focused on the bottom line, but instead they focused on serving the customer.
That was incredibly powerful for them. And we encourage the same with our operating companies. Now we wouldn't tell our operating companies how to serve their customers.
And they know how to serve their customers best and they are the ones that are on the front lines talking to their customers every day.
But absolutely we would encourage our companies to do whatever it takes to take care of our customers.
We're in a business that's a highly recurring revenue business with very long customer relationships.
And so it is economically foolish to do something in the short term that might make you an extra dollar that in any way, you know, threatens the trust that that customer has with our business.
And so we very much would encourage the same and we would celebrate, you know, similar stories as Home Depot.
I hope we can rack up more stories like the ones that Home Depot has over the years. It's truly an inspiration.
The examples that they have of serving the customer.
As we talked about, the founders spent a lot of time in the stores. They were both helping out with stuff in the stores.
And they were also disguising as customers just walking into stores and seeing if someone would help them, if how they would be treated.
And that is not really decentralized in a way. How do you go about it? Do you also go out in the operating businesses or how do you actually check what's happening out there?
So we're structured a little bit differently. I do think you need to be in touch with what's going on on the ground. And so from my vantage point, I personally spent a lot of time on acquisitions.
And so I love to go visit business owners and go see how they operate their business go learn from new acquisition opportunities.
And when I'm on the road, if there's an opportunity to go visit one of our operating companies, it's close by I love to go visit one of our operating companies.
But we're very decentralized. We're very much empowering our operating companies and our vertical CEOs.
We also have a high degree of trust in what's going on the ground and letting the leaders locally lead their business.
And when we look at our vertical CEOs, they're more focused on the organic growth side of things.
They're on the road much more often specifically focus on well, I'm on the road focus. I'm an a they're on the road focused on their operating companies.
And so they're they're regularly getting in front of our businesses, engaging with them, learning from them, you're checking in, not sharing best practices that are learning from other companies.
